title: Journey 2: The Jacket Comes Back
basis: Reconstructed from the published chapter (posts/38-journey-return-and-exchange/index.md) and its former spec.md, whose Non-goals, Modalities, Open questions, Decision log, Sources and Changelog are carried over. One spec paragraph per unit of the chapter, plus the units the contract asks for and the published chapter did not have (the thesis paragraph p03, the roadmap p04 and the conclusion's synthesis p61); these are listed under decision_log.

know: Which system owns each fact of a return in the late-2027 design (the OMS the order, eligibility and the return record; the WMS inspection, disposition and physical stock; the availability service what may be sold again; the PSP the refund; the ERP the credit note and the new invoice), and the twelve steps from request to reconciliation.

The EU clocks a return runs on (14 days to withdraw from possession, a refund within 14 days of the notice, the right to withhold until the goods or evidence of sending arrive), the four dispositions, the three release policies for an exchange, and why refunds are asynchronous and can fail days after acceptance.

Kestrel & Pine's cases on this path: Eva's exchange (requested 19 April 2027, inspected and graded resellable 22 April, size L shipped that day; a credit note of −€199 against the original invoice and a new invoice of €199), the Double Refund of January 2027 (212 returns, €19,400 refunded twice) and its February 2027 fix, the 190 Black Friday returns refunded about €3,000 too much, and the marketplace and store variants.
believe: A return is finished only when stock, money and books agree.
The refund belongs to the warehouse's disposition event, with one writer and one key.
An exchange is a return plus a new order, never an edit.
can_do: Count the systems that can call the PSP's refund API in their own landscape and name the key on the request.
Design an exchange and a refund so that a returned unit raises sellable stock only on its disposition and the books record a credit note.

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture; most of all the engineer or product manager who has read the capability chapters and Journey 1 and now needs to see returns, refunds and credit notes as one path. Finance and operations readers get the money-and-books half in plain words.

Kestrel & Pine, its people, its 2026 and January 2027 incidents in outline and the names of the sixteen failure patterns.

From Part I: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines (money, goods, returns), 'system', 'the shop platform' for the hosted product and 'commerce platform' for the whole set of systems, business models and the four scale stages, the capability map, bounded context, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation, the Waypoint decisions W1 to W8.
Glosses already given: PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, EDI, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL, order hub and order management system, availability service, D2C, B2B, PIM, POS.

From Parts II and III: product, variant, SKU and GTIN with one owning system per attribute; prices frozen at order placement; promotions as data, discounts allocated to lines; available-to-promise, one writer each for on hand and committed; authorization, capture, settlement and payout, refunds as new payments; one order record with three status lines; tax from three facts, one invoice per shipment, credit notes as the only correction, the monthly match of invoices, payouts and bank lines.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given refunds paid twice, the reader names two writers and no key as the cause and plans one writer, one key and a daily match, rather than retraining support.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A brand's returns app refunds customers through the shop platform after the warehouse inspects a return, which takes two to five days. Support agents, seeing a carrier scan at the warehouse and no refund yet, refund impatient customers in the payment provider's console. At month-end finance finds hundreds of returns credited twice. Using only this chapter: what went wrong, and what should change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Two systems could write the refund and neither request named the return, so the payment provider accepted both. One writer may call the refund API (the returns app, later the OMS when it holds the return record), with support's console access read-only; each request carries the return id as its idempotency key; the refund is raised by the warehouse's disposition event, not the request or the carrier scan; its state (requested, accepted, refunded or failed) is driven by webhooks and confirmed by a fetched status; a daily job matches every PSP refund to a refunded return, every refunded return to a credit note and every credit note to an invoice; and support sees which of receipt, inspection and refund has happened.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say why an exchange is not an edit and when a returned unit may be sold again.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer exchanges a €199 jacket in size M for size L. The team proposes to change the original order line from M to L, ship the L once the parcel is scanned at the dock, and add the M back to stock at that scan. Using only this chapter: what is wrong with the plan, and what should happen?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The M was picked, invoiced and paid for, so editing the line leaves an invoice for a jacket the customer no longer has. An exchange is a return plus a new order: at request time a held order for one L is created at the original frozen price with a €0 balance and the unit is committed in the availability service; the disposition releases it (release on scan or an instant exchange are other policies with their own risks). The ERP issues a credit note of −€199 against the original invoice and a new invoice of €199, which net to zero. The M raises sellable stock only when inspection grades it restockable, never at the dock scan, because some returns need processing or cannot be resold.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can compute a return's legal dates and say what changes when the return comes through a marketplace or a store.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Goods are delivered on 15 April; the customer gives notice of withdrawal on 19 April and drops the parcel at a carrier point on 20 April. Using only this chapter: by when must the merchant refund, from when may it no longer withhold the refund, and what changes if the same jacket was bought through a marketplace or is returned in a store?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The withdrawal window runs 14 days from possession, to 29 April; the refund is due within 14 days of the notice, by 3 May; the merchant may withhold it until it has the goods or evidence of sending, so the carrier's acceptance scan on 20 April ends the withholding right. The OMS computes delivery, notice, evidence of sending and refund dates per line. On a marketplace the policy is the marketplace's; the OMS must accept returns it did not create and refunds it did not issue, keyed on the marketplace's return id, with the money state 'refunded externally'. In a store the POS records the return against the order number, the stock lands in that store's location and the refund goes to the original payment method through the same single writer, not as cash.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: That receiving a returned parcel does not say whether the item can be resold, whether the replacement is reserved or whether money is due, decisions owned by different systems; that if each treats its own step as the finished return a customer can be refunded twice or wait for an unsecured replacement; that a return is three flows (goods, money, books), the refund is triggered by the warehouse's disposition with one writer and one key, and an exchange is a return plus a new order, with marketplace and store returns as variants; Kestrel & Pine's return figures (72,000 return parcels in 2026, 24% of items, 28% exchanges, 61% resold as new) beside the NRF's; Eva's exchange from 19 April, followed through authorization, transport back, inspection, replacement and accounting. thesis.question: How does a return and exchange travel back through the systems, and where do the money, the stock and the books part ways?
thesis.claim: A return travels back on one path until the warehouse's disposition event, which alone releases three flows with three owners: stock in the warehouse system, money through the payment provider (or, for an exchange, a held new order at the price on the original order line) and books through a credit note in the ERP. Exactly one system calls the refund API, keyed on the return id, and an exchange is never an edit of the original order or invoice.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a return is a refund button: the returns app or support refunds when the customer asks or the carrier scans the parcel, stock goes back on the shelf when the parcel arrives, and an exchange is an edit of the original order line.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim lets exactly one system call the refund API, keys every refund on the return, raises stock and settlement only on the disposition, and matches refunds to credit notes daily. In January 2027 Kestrel & Pine refunded 212 returns twice, €19,400, because the returns portal and support in the PSP console could both refund with no key naming the return, and finance found it at month-end; in February it made the portal the single writer, set support's console access to read-only and started a daily match. Eva's exchange, requested on 19 April 2027 and graded resellable on 22 April, ships size L the same day and leaves a credit note of −€199 and a new invoice of €199 that net to zero.
thesis.how_why: EU law gives the consumer 14 days to withdraw from possession and the merchant 14 days from the notice to refund, withholdable only until the goods or evidence of sending arrive, so the return needs dates per line from the order record. Refunds are asynchronous and can fail days after acceptance, and a PSP accepts two requests that carry no shared key, so the count of writers and the key decide whether money goes out once. Only inspection knows whether a unit is sellable (39% of Kestrel & Pine's returned items in 2026 were not graded new), so stock raised at the dock scan promises units in a repair bin; and an issued invoice is immutable, so the books change only by credit note.

supporting_claims.claim: Many systems hold a piece of one return, and that is normal: each fact (the order and the return record, eligibility, inspection and disposition, physical stock, sellable stock, the refund, the credit note) has exactly one system of record, and the return follows one path from request to inspection that each of them sees.

The warehouse's disposition event, and nothing earlier, releases the three flows: a returned unit raises sellable stock only when inspection grades it restockable, the held exchange or the refund is released by the same event, and the books follow it.

Exactly one system may call the refund API, with the return id as its idempotency key, inside the EU's 14-day refund clock; because refunds are asynchronous and can fail days later, the money state is driven by the PSP's webhooks and a fetched status, never assumed.

An exchange is a return plus a new order at the price frozen on the original order, never an edit: the books record a credit note against the original invoice and a new invoice that net to zero, and a daily match ties every refund to a return, a credit note and an invoice.

Marketplace and store returns are the same flow with a different first step: the OMS accepts returns it did not create and refunds it did not issue, and a store return lands stock in the store and refunds the original payment through the same single writer.

Each handoff on the way back needs a key and a delivery style matched to its clock, and on the January 2027 landscape, where one return lived in three records and the refund had two writers and no key, the path broke at those handoffs: the Double Refund paid 212 returns twice while every system did what it was built to do.

role.contribution: Walks Eva's exchange, with the refund as its alternative and the Double Refund as its failure path, back through the late-2027 design, separates the goods, money and books flows released by one disposition event, and compares the January 2027 path.

flow.rationale: The return's facts and owners come first because every step refers to them; the step table then gives the whole way back, and the sections walk it in the order the return lives it (request, transit, inspection, then the exchange, the refund alternative and the books that the inspection releases), closing the main path with what each of its handoffs requires. Only then do the last three sections step outside it: two variants that change only the first step, the same return on the January 2027 landscape (to which the store variant's January gap leads), and four failures with their detection. Moving the variants before the walk would change a first step the reader has not seen; moving the failures or the January comparison earlier would describe joins the reader has not yet met; putting the requirements after the variants would separate them from the path they describe.

hook.content: A customer returns a jacket and asks for a larger size. Receiving the parcel does not tell the merchant whether the original can be sold again, whether the replacement is reserved or whether a financial adjustment is due; those decisions belong to different systems, and if each treats its own step as the completed return, the customer can be refunded twice or wait for a replacement that was never secured.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Editing the line from M to L would leave an invoice for a jacket Eva no longer has, because the M was picked, invoiced and paid for.

sections.heading: The Refund Alternative: One Writer, One Key
sections.controlling_idea: Had Eva asked for her money, the same disposition would release one refund request from one writer, keyed on the return id, whose result arrives later and may still fail.

advances_thesis.how: States the trigger, the writer, the key and the asynchronous money state.

flow.rationale: The branch, then the trigger, then who writes, then with what key, then what happens after the request is accepted and the state that tracks it: each answer assumes the one before.

transition_in.carries_over: The exchange released by the disposition.
transition_in.introduces: The refund the same event would release.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: If Eva asks for her money, everything up to the disposition event is the same, and the event releases a €199 refund instead.
The refund is triggered by the disposition, not the request or the scan, which keeps money and goods in one causal chain and leaves eleven days of margin to the 3 May deadline.

evidence.what: Notice 19 April, deadline 3 May, inspection 22 April: eleven days of margin.
evidence.shows: The trigger is safe only while the dock inspects quickly.

transition_in.carries_over: The refund released by the disposition.
transition_in.introduces: Why the disposition and not an earlier event.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the target design exactly one system, the OMS, raises the refund through the shop platform's refund API to the PSP; support, the portal and the ERP cannot, and support's console access is read-only.

evidence.what: The OMS as the single refund writer once it holds return records (Q4 2027); support's PSP console read-only.
evidence.shows: The design counts writers: one.

transition_in.introduces: Who may raise it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The request carries the return id as its idempotency key so that a retry does nothing twice; the PSP's own duplicate protection is a backstop, not the design.

evidence.what: Stripe saves the first response to a key; Mollie 'blocks duplicate refunds made in a short time frame' and asks merchants to 'do not retry automatically'.
evidence.source: Stripe and Mollie documentation, n.d., accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: Providers expect a key and a status check from the merchant.

transition_in.introduces: One key.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Refunds are asynchronous and can fail late: accepting a request starts work that continues, and Adyen and Stripe document refunds that fail days after a success message and reach the customer days later, while for iDEAL the refund is a new transfer to the shopper's bank account.

transition_in.introduces: What happens after it is accepted.

evidence.what: Adyen: 'the refund process is asynchronous', a refund 'can fail after you received' the success webhook, refunded-reversed for iDEAL; Stripe: 'approximately 5-10 business days', fees not returned.
evidence.source: Adyen and Stripe documentation, n.d., accessed 2026-11
evidence.shows: Late failure is documented behaviour, not an edge case.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: So the return's money state is a small machine of its own, requested, accepted, refunded or failed, driven by webhooks and confirmed by a fetched status, and Eva's messages follow it.

evidence.what: Figure 4: one writer and one key, the PSP's answer by webhook confirmed by a fetch, the ERP matching credit notes to payout lines, and the dotted second writer the Double Refund closed.
evidence.shows: The refund path as one writer, one key and a confirmed state.

transition_in.introduces: The state machine that tracks it.

sections.heading: The Books: Credit Note, New Invoice, Reconciliation
sections.controlling_idea: The books change only by credit note: an exchange is a credit note and a new invoice that net to zero, a refund pairs the credit note with a PSP refund, and a daily three-leg match ties them together.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the third flow and the reconciliation that makes the three agree.

flow.rationale: The rule (no edit), then the exchange's two documents, then the refund variant, then the match that checks all of them. The match cannot be read before the documents it matches.

transition_in.introduces: The books, the third flow.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The third flow is the books: the original invoice stays as it is, so when the OMS reports the return settled the ERP issues a credit note of −€199 against it for the jacket line.

evidence.what: Original invoice net €194.21, VAT €40.79, gross €235.00; credit note −€199.00 (net −€164.46, VAT −€34.54).
evidence.shows: The correction is a new document with exact figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An exchange is two documents that net to zero: the credit note and a new €199 invoice for #1072455-X1, so Eva's bank statement shows nothing while the ledger shows the whole history.

transition_in.introduces: Its partner document for the exchange.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The refund variant pairs the same credit note with a refund at the PSP, reversing the revenue recognized at delivery.

transition_in.introduces: The refund variant's pair.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Reconciliation is daily, not monthly: since February 2027, after the Double Refund, a daily job matches PSP refunds to the shop platform's to catch any duplicate the key lets through, and in the target design the match has three legs (refund to return, return to credit note, credit note to invoice).

evidence.what: Daily job from February 2027 matching PSP refunds on order number and amount, exceptions to finance.
evidence.shows: The match runs on the clock of the failure it catches.

transition_in.carries_over: Documents and refunds in two systems.
transition_in.introduces: The check that they agree.

evidence.what: Six handoffs from portal to OMS through OMS to ERP, each with its key and style under W5.
evidence.shows: Every join has a key and a style matched to its clock.

evidence.shows: Two marketplace cases with different owners of the goods.

sections.heading: When It Goes Wrong Along This Path
sections.controlling_idea: Four failures on the way back each have a mechanism at a join, a detection and a recovery, and the Double Refund shows what two writers and no key cost.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: The parcel at Duiven told nobody whether the jacket could be sold, whether the L was reserved or whether money was due; walked back step by step, each answer has one owner and waits for one event. The L was committed when Eva asked, the disposition released it with the stock and the credit note, and no refund was involved. On the January 2027 landscape the same systems held the same pieces, but three return records and two refund writers without a key paid 212 returns twice.
conclusion.so_what: A merchant that makes the disposition the only trigger, allows one refund writer with the return id as key and matches refunds to credit notes daily closes each return in agreement instead of reconciling it by hand at month-end.

callback.to: The introduction's hook: a returned jacket whose arrival does not say whether it can be resold, whether the replacement is reserved or whether money is due, with a double refund or an unsecured replacement as the risk.
callback.how: The reader can now name the owner and the event behind each of the three answers, and the joins where the two risks arise.

takeaway.content: Count the systems that can call the refund API; if the answer is not one, fix that first, then make the disposition the only trigger for stock, money and the books and measure the time from dock scan to disposition every day.

hand_off.carries_over: Journeys 1 and 2: a consumer who orders at a checkout, pays at once and receives a parcel, and the same Duiven stock and systems behind her.
hand_off.introduces: A buyer that is a company: an order that arrives as a message nobody typed, goods that leave on pallets with a despatch advice, and money that arrives thirty days later against an invoice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The parcel at Duiven answered none of the opening's three questions by itself; walked back, each answer has one owner and waits for the disposition, which on the January 2027 landscape had three return records and two refund writers behind it, so a merchant that makes the disposition the only trigger, allows one refund writer with one key and matches daily closes returns in agreement instead of at month-end.

evidence.what: The opening's three questions set against Eva's late-2027 exchange and the January 2027 Double Refund.
evidence.shows: The reader can now say where a return goes right or wrong.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Established: a return is three flows with three owners, as Shopify, commercetools and every ERP model it; refunds are asynchronous and can fail late, as Adyen, Stripe and Mollie document; and EU law fixes the clocks.
